# toolgz

> Compresses LLM tool definitions to reclaim context window. Zero runtime dependencies,
> TypeScript, Apache-2.0. Works with any model and any framework: it transforms a tool
> array before you send it, and translates the model's call back afterwards.

**This file is written for a coding agent integrating toolgz into a project.** It is
prescriptive on purpose. If you are contributing to toolgz itself, read `AGENTS.md` in the
repository instead — different audience, different rules.

Installed copy lives at `node_modules/toolgz/llms.txt`. Full prose docs: `README.md`.

---

## The whole integration, correctly

```ts
import { compress, recommendLevel, forAnthropic } from "toolgz";

// 1. Decide the level ONCE, at startup — not per request.
const { level } = recommendLevel(myTools);
const c = compress(myTools, { level });

// 2. Send c.tools instead of your tool array, and append the preamble to your system prompt.
const { tools, system } = forAnthropic(c);

// 3. Translate every tool call back before you dispatch.
for (const block of res.content.filter((b) => b.type === "tool_use")) {
  const r = c.resolve(block.name, block.input);
  if (r.kind === "call") {
    const out = await myDispatch(r.name, r.args);      // real name, real args
    results.push({ type: "tool_result", tool_use_id: block.id, content: JSON.stringify(out) });
  } else if (r.kind === "meta") {
    // toolgz answered a lookup itself. DO NOT dispatch. Return its text to the model.
    results.push({ type: "tool_result", tool_use_id: block.id, content: r.result });
  } else {
    // Recoverable by design: hand the message back and the model retries.
    results.push({ type: "tool_result", tool_use_id: block.id, content: `Error: ${r.message}`, is_error: true });
  }
}
```

Those three steps are the entire contract. `myDispatch` receives exactly what it received
before toolgz existed.

## Rules that are not optional

1. **`resolve()` every tool call.** At level 3 the model emits opaque codes (`t(f="a0")`),
   so dispatching `block.name` directly will fail or dispatch the wrong tool. Route
   everything through `resolve()` even at level 0, so the level becomes a one-line change.

2. **Handle all three `kind` values.** `call` → dispatch. `meta` → toolgz already answered
   a lookup; return `r.result` to the model and dispatch nothing. `error` → return
   `r.message` to the model as an error tool_result; do **not** throw. The `error` path is
   the recovery mechanism, not a failure.

3. **Send the system preamble.** At level 3 the tool map lives in the system prompt. Drop
   it and the model has no idea what any code means. It is `""` at levels 0–1, so
   appending it unconditionally is always safe.

4. **`compress()` never changes level on its own.** `compress(tools)` is level 1 forever,
   2 tools or 500. `recommendLevel()` *advises*; you pass its answer in as `{ level }`.
   Deliberate: level 3 moves argument validation from the provider to toolgz, which is not
   a change to make behind a caller's back.

5. **Leave `validate` on** (the default). Levels 2–3 give up the provider's constrained
   decoding, so toolgz validating against the original schema is what catches malformed
   arguments. On a weak model, disabling it converts roughly half of all runs from a
   recovered retry into a bad dispatch.

6. **Compress once, reuse the result.** `compress()` is deterministic — same tools in,
   byte-identical payload out — so the output is prompt-cache friendly. Recomputing per
   request is wasted work; changing the tool list mid-conversation invalidates the cache
   and strands codes the model has already seen.

## Choosing a level

Ask, don't guess: `recommendLevel(myTools)` returns `{ level, reason }` — **0, 1 or 3**,
never 2 and never 4. When it says 3 and that map would be mostly lookalike lines, the
reason says how many and points at `npx toolgz compile`.

`level: 0` means *leave the tools alone*: level 1 would make this block larger, and it is
too small for level 3 to be worth giving up provider-side validation. Level 1 is not
unconditionally free — it saves by stripping prose, so on tools whose descriptions are
already one short sentence it adds ~15% instead. Do not override a 0 without measuring.

| Level | Wire | Names | Provider enforces schema | When |
|:-:|---|:-:|:-:|---|
| 0 | unchanged | real | yes | A/B control. Route through `resolve()` anyway so other levels are a one-line change |
| **1** | one native tool each, flattened schemas | real | **yes** | **default.** 39% in tokens on real MCP tools; **inflates ~15% on already-terse ones** |
| 2 | one compound tool per namespace | real | no | only when something downstream must read real op names off the raw request. 4,408 tokens vs level 3's 2,947 and 16 malformed args vs 0 over 60 runs each. NOT dominated on size past ~300 tools — level 3's map grows per tool and level 2 overtakes it — but argument quality is why to avoid it |
| **3** | one dispatcher + one lookup | codes | no | **large tool sets.** 95.6% of the tool block. Weak when tool names collide — check `stats.ambiguousMapLines` |
| **4** | one dispatcher + one lookup | real names | no | when level 3's map is mostly lookalikes. Bigger than 3 on purpose; needs `compiled` |

Measured head-to-head in one sweep (96 runs, 96/96 tasks, 0 hallucinated names): level 3 is
smaller on every provider, level 4 uses fewer turns and lookups — on `claude-opus-5`, 4.1 →
3.3 turns and 1.5 → 0.5 lookups. That recovers about a quarter of level 3's size advantage,
not all of it. **Default to 3.** Go to 4 only when `stats.ambiguousMapLines` is high.

`recommendLevel` returns 0, 1 or 3. Never 2 (dominated on every axis) and never 4 (needs a
compiled artifact the caller may not have) — but when it says 3 and that map would be mostly
lookalike lines, the reason says how many and names the fix.

The switch is the **size** of the level-1 block, not the tool count — threshold 10,000
tokens (~5% of a 200k window). A tool is 20 to 460 tokens depending on schema verbosity,
so 40 real MCP tools cross it while 72 one-parameter tools do not.

Level 2 is dominated by level 3 on accuracy — 16 malformed arguments against zero over 60
runs each — and is
never recommended. It stays in the API for callers who need real operation names.

## Before shipping level 3, check the map is not all lookalikes

```ts
const c = compress(myTools, { level: 3 });
c.stats.ambiguousMapLines      // lines sharing a body with another line
c.stats.largestLookalikeGroup  // size of the biggest such group; 1 is ideal
```

At level 3 the map is all the model has. If many tools render to the same line — common
when tools are named `manage_x` and all take one `operation` argument — the name becomes
the only signal and the model keyword-matches. Measured on a real 60-tool registry:
`name+required` gave 44/60 ambiguous lines and the model picked the wrong tool 3/3;
`mapStyle: "signature"` gave 2/60 and 0 wrong picks, for 4,242 more tokens.

**A high number means switch to `mapStyle: "signature"`.** Do not ignore it.

## Level 4 — a map a model compiled for you

Levels 0-3 derive the map from your schema, so they can only rearrange information that is
already there. When tool names collide there is nothing left to rearrange. Level 4 has a
model rewrite the corpus first:

```python
def article_append(article_id,content):"add to end, keeping existing text; use over article_update"
```

Bring your own model — the library never imports an SDK:

```ts
const { compiled } = await compileTools(myTools, {
  complete: async ({ system, user }) => yourClient.run(system, user),
});
compress(myTools, { level: 4, compiled });
```

Or `npx toolgz compile --tools ./tools.json --out ./toolmap.json`.

- Every compiled line is verified against the real schema — no renamed tool, no invented
  parameter, no dropped required parameter. Failures are discarded, not shipped.
- A tool with no compiled entry falls back to a bare signature line and is counted in
  `stats.uncompiledTools`. Check it.
- `compress(tools, { level: 4 })` without `compiled` throws. There is no silent empty map.
- Measured over **180 live runs on four frontier models**: every task completed, zero
  hallucinated tool names, one recovered malformed argument. See docs/RESULTS.md Round 8.
- Staleness is caught at compress() time — every compiled line is re-verified against the
  live schema, so a map compiled before a tool changed shape has that line **dropped** and
  listed in `stats.staleCompiledTools`. The schema is the fingerprint; there is nothing to
  maintain.
- `requireCompiled: true` turns a partial map into a throw. Use it in CI.
- **What it cannot do:** check whether a docstring is *true*. Verification covers the
  contract, not the claim.

## Parameter shapes are derived, not guessed

Every level that renders a signature — 1, 3 with `mapStyle: "signature"`, and 4 — shows
container shapes taken from your schema:

```
analyze_consolidation(shipments:[],truckSpecs:{})
gdrive_sheets_append_rows(spreadsheet_id,range,values:array[],value_input_option?:RAW|USER_ENTERED)
```

`k:a|b|c` for an enum, `k:[]` for an array, `k:{}` for an object. This is not cosmetic: over
144 runs on a suite built to test argument shape, **every malformed argument landed on the
one arm whose map omits shapes** — `mapStyle: "name+required"` — on three separate
providers, and it also spent 0.77 lookups per run against 0.08.

**Upgrading to 0.6.x may make your level-4 map bigger, and that is the fix working.** The
shapes are derived at compress time, so you get full coverage with no recompile. Whether the
wire grows or shrinks depends on your existing artifact: if its docstrings already spelled
shapes out in prose, recompiling removes the duplication and the map shrinks (−19% here); if
they did not, deriving adds shapes the map never had and it grows (+14.7% on one external
catalogue). Recompile either way — it is the only way to stop paying for prose that is now
redundant.

**If your tools take objects or arrays, do not use `mapStyle: "name+required"` at level 3.**
Use `"signature"`, or level 4. And do not write shapes into a compiled docstring: the
signature is regenerated from the schema, so restating them wastes characters that should
carry purpose.

## Enforcement: what a dispatcher can and cannot have

Levels 2, 3 and 4 give up provider-side argument checking. That is structural — the sampler
cannot enforce a schema it was not sent, and not sending it is the compression.

- **No enforcement of any kind is available on a dispatcher.** Argument enforcement would
  need a discriminated union on `f`, which the Anthropic API rejects at the top level of an
  `input_schema` (measured at +112,488 characters before the API refused it). Constraining
  `f` to an enum of tool names is legal but was measured and removed: +47% to +70% of the
  level-3 map, zero hallucinated names prevented across 192 runs, and it caused grok-4.5 to
  answer with no tool call and no error — twice.
- **If you need real enforcement, use level 1** — with or without a compiled map. Native
  tools, real schemas, provider enforcing everything. `compress(tools, { level: 1, compiled })`
  swaps each tool's prose for the compiled docstring at about the same size (+2.2%).
- **Do not set `signaturePrefix: false` to shrink level 1 unless you have measured it.** It
  buys ~16% by removing the only place the parameter inventory appears in prose — level 1
  strips per-property descriptions. Measured on one real registry: selection accuracy fell
  68.9% -> 60.0% on Opus, 57.8% -> 44.4% on Kimi, and a previously clean arm started
  inventing parameters. The saving IS the inventory.

## Two hard facts about level 3

1. **Nothing schema-encoded reaches the model.** The wire is `t(f, a)` and `q(c, s)` with
   generic argument objects; no parameter name from the registry appears in them. The
   schema is used only for toolgz's validation, and the model sees it only via a `q()`
   expansion. Contracts in `required[]`, in conditionals, or in parameter descriptions are
   invisible. **Behavioural policy must go in the system prompt.**
2. **Audit and logging must read `resolve()` output.** Real tool names never hit the wire.
   A raw-request log shows `t`, `q` and opaque codes. `resolve()` returns the real name and
   byte-identical args — log from there.

## Conditionally required parameters

Supported, and enforced by `validate` at every level:

```json
"allOf": [{ "if": { "properties": { "operation": { "const": "delete" } } },
            "then": { "required": ["_confirmed"] } }]
```

Use this instead of putting the key in `required[]` when a tool is compound — an
unconditional `required` would reject `{operation:"list"}` too. `const` and `enum`
conditions work, `if`/`then` may be top-level or inside `allOf`, and branches accumulate.
**`else`, nested conditionals, `not` and `dependentRequired` are ignored, not enforced** —
and a condition that cannot be evaluated never adds a requirement.

## Provider adapters — pick the right one

```ts
forAnthropic(c, { cache?, ttl? })  // → { tools, system }        Messages API
forOpenAI(c)                       // → { tools, systemPreamble } /v1/chat/completions
forOpenAIResponses(c)              // → { tools, systemPreamble } /v1/responses
forGemini(c)                       // → { tools, systemPreamble } generateContent
```

Two mistakes that produce confusing provider errors:

- **OpenAI has two incompatible tool shapes.** `/v1/chat/completions` wants nested
  `{type, function:{…}}`; `/v1/responses` wants flat `{type, name, …}`. If you set
  reasoning effort on a GPT-5.x model you must use `/v1/responses`, therefore
  `forOpenAIResponses`. Using the wrong adapter is rejected at the API.
- **Gemini returns ONE wrapper object,** not one entry per tool. Read
  `tools[0].functionDeclarations.length`; `tools.length` is always 1.

`forGemini` also repairs three schema forms Gemini rejects with a 400: an array-valued
`type`, `type: "array"` with no `items`, and a non-string `enum`. Constraints stripped to
satisfy Gemini are still enforced by `resolve()` against your original schema — nothing is
silently dropped.

xAI is OpenAI-compatible: use `forOpenAI` with `baseURL: "https://api.x.ai/v1"`. **xAI
caps tool arrays at 350**; other providers accept 1,200+. Level 3 sends 2 either way.

## Model-specific behaviour

Pass an exact model id and toolgz uses the best *measured* map style for it:

```ts
compress(myTools, { level: 3, model: "gpt-5.6-sol", objective: "cost" });
```

| Model | `objective: "cost"` | Measured vs default |
|---|---|---:|
| `gpt-5.6-sol` | `explicit` | −20.7% |
| `gemini-3.1-pro-preview` | `explicit` | −15.4% |
| `claude-opus-5` | `explicit` | −9.0% |
| `grok-4.5` | *(no entry)* | `explicit` is **+13.2%** there |

- Model ids are **exact, never families**. A result for `gpt-5.6-sol` says nothing about
  `gpt-5.7`. An unknown model gets the conservative default — absence of evidence, not a
  prediction.
- The default objective is `occupancy`, which has **no** entries: nothing beat the default
  by more than 3.1% on that axis, under the 5% effect-size floor. Only `cost` has rows.
- This is the one thing the library picks for you, and only when you pass `model`. A map
  style is a pure encoding choice, so a better one cannot change results. The *level*
  can — which is why that stays explicit.
- Do not set `mapStyle` by hand unless you have measured your own workload. Prefer
  `model` + `objective`.

## MCP servers

`tools/list` returns `{ name, description, inputSchema }` per tool — exactly what
`compress()` accepts. **There is no adapter layer.** Merge the arrays from every server
and pass them in.

`input_schema` and `inputSchema` are both accepted, so Anthropic-shaped and MCP-shaped
tools can be mixed.

Watch for name collisions when merging catalogues from independent servers. If two tool
names normalise identically, toolgz refuses to alias either one rather than guess — the
map code still works.

## API surface

```ts
compress(tools, options?) → CompressResult
recommendLevel(tools, namespaceOf?) → { level, reason, toolCount, namespaceCount, opsPerNamespace }
selectMapStyle(options) → { mapStyle, requestedMapStyle?, fallbackReason? }   // pure
```

`CompressOptions`: `level`, `mapStyle`, `namespaceOf`, `aliasOf`, `signaturePrefix`,
`compiled`, `requireCompiled`, `searchLimit`, `validate`, `model`,
`objective`.

`CompressStats`: `level`, `mapStyle`, `requestedMapStyle`, `fallbackReason`, `toolCount`,
`wireToolCount`, `originalChars`, `compressedChars`, `savedPct`, `ambiguousMapLines`,
`largestLookalikeGroup`, `uncompiledTools`, `staleCompiledTools`,
`orphanedCompiledEntries`.

Compile-time helpers: `compileTools(tools, { complete })` → `{ compiled, rejected,
danglingReferences, stats }`, and `verifyCompiledLine(line, tool)` → `null` when the line
is safe to ship or a reason when it is not. Use the second if you compile your own way —
it is what refuses a renamed tool, an invented parameter or a dropped required one.

`signaturePrefix` (level 1, default true) controls the `name(a,b?) — ` prefix on each
description. Setting it false makes level 1 smaller — 45.1% → 55.3% in characters on real MCP tools —
and measured cheaper on Gemini, OpenAI and xAI over 64 runs. On `claude-opus-5` it was
**+3.8% dearer** because turns rose 3.88 → 4.63. Safe either way (zero malformed
arguments on both arms); not universally cheaper. Do not set it without measuring your
own workload.

`CompressResult`: `tools`, `systemPreamble`, `cachePreamble`, `resolve()`, `codeFor()`,
`encodeCallForTest()`, `stats`.

`stats`: `level`, `mapStyle`, `requestedMapStyle`, `fallbackReason`, `toolCount`,
`wireToolCount`, `originalChars`, `compressedChars`, `savedPct`.

`namespaceOf` must return `{ ns, op }`, **not** a bare string. Returning a string throws
with a corrected example — it used to fail silently and produce a plausible-looking but
wrong map.

## Things to tell the user, not assume

- **`savedPct` is a CHARACTER saving**, a few points optimistic against tokens. Providers
  charge a fixed framing cost per tool definition that character counting cannot see. For
  any published figure, measure with the provider's own token counter.
- **Never use `tiktoken` to count Claude tokens** — it is OpenAI's tokenizer and is wrong
  for Claude by 15–20%+. Use Anthropic's `count_tokens`.
- **Token saving ≠ cost saving.** Prompt caching already makes tool tokens cheap; the claim
  here is context-window *occupancy*. Cost follows by a variable amount, and on OpenAI —
  where reasoning output dominates the bill — it was as little as 7%.
- **Level 3 costs turns.** Roughly 0.3–1.7 lookup calls per task, about half an extra turn.
  If latency matters more than context, stay at level 1.
- **Below the frontier tier, argument formatting degrades at level 3.** On Haiku 4.5, 17 of
  30 runs produced a malformed argument — all caught by `validate` and recovered, no task
  lost, but that is the known edge. Tool *choice* did not degrade.

## Do not

- Do not dispatch `block.name` without `resolve()`.
- Do not throw on `kind: "error"` — return it to the model.
- Do not dispatch on `kind: "meta"`.
- Do not omit `systemPreamble` at level 3.
- Do not set `validate: false` to silence a malformed-argument error; fix the schema.
- Do not call `compress()` inside the request loop.
- Do not report `savedPct` as a token or cost saving.
- Do not assume a level was chosen for you.
